analysis.one_liner: Caps pay raises at big bailout banks to the federal employee raise.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced in March 2009, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2008 financial crisis, taxpayers gave hundreds of billions of dollars to banks under the TARP bailout. This bill would have required any financial institution that received more than $10 billion in TARP money to limit pay raises for its executives and employees to the same annual percentage raise federal civil servants get. It was introduced in the House in March 2009 and sent to the Financial Services Committee, where it sat without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the bailouts. The bill would have tied executive and employee pay at the largest bailout recipients to the modest raises ordinary federal workers receive, rather than allowing compensation to rebound while the public was still on the hook for the rescue.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any financial institution that received more than $10 billion in TARP assistance from raising any officer's, director's, or employee's pay by more than the federal civil service pay increase for the year [S2][S3].
Applies to institutions receiving TARP assistance after enactment, tying the pay of executives at the largest bailout recipients to the same raise scale as rank-and-file government workers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Highly compensated officers, directors, and employees at the biggest TARP recipient banks, who would have seen raises limited to the federal employee increase instead of market-level or bonus-driven increases.

drawbacks.text: The cap covers only institutions that received more than $10 billion under TARP, so smaller bailout recipients and banks that later repaid aid would escape it, limiting how much accountability it actually delivered [S2][S3].

A strict pay-raise ceiling set by the civil service schedule could make it harder for bailed-out banks to retain and recruit executives at market rates, which critics of compensation caps argued could weaken the very institutions taxpayers were trying to stabilize.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was narrow but straightforward: it tied pay raises at the largest bailout recipients to the raise ordinary federal employees get, a direct response to public anger over Wall Street compensation following a taxpayer-funded rescue. Its main weaknesses were its narrow coverage (only institutions over $10 billion in TARP aid) and the risk that rigid pay caps complicate executive retention at banks still recovering. The cost to the public of the limits was small; the benefit was accountability for institutions kept afloat by public money.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2009, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Wilson of Ohio introduced the TARP Wage Accountability Act in the House on March 18, 2009 [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears in the bill's history [S5].
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executives and employees of the large banks that received more than $10 billion in TARP aid came out ahead: their compensation was never capped, because the bill never left committee. Taxpayers got no additional pay accountability for the bailout funds they provided.

for.name: Rep. Charles A. Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 18, 2009, to cap pay raises at the largest TARP recipients [S1][S3][S5].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored and cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Large banks and financial institutions receiving TARP assistance
industries.note: The bill would have limited annual pay increases for officers, directors, and employees at institutions that received more than $10 billion in TARP funds to the federal civil service raise. The industry's interest in avoiding such caps ran against taxpayers' interest in accountability for bailout money.
